w3.title: Change Without Fear
w3.subtitle: Automation, release engineering, %1% and configuration: most outages start with a change.
w3.intro:
Roughly 70% of outages are triggered by a change to a running system (the %1% book's oft-quoted figure). This world is about making change safe rather than rare: the hierarchy of automation, hermetic and self-service releases, progressive rollouts with real %2% analysis, and the surprisingly dangerous topic of configuration. Sources: %3% book chapters 7, 8 and 9; workbook chapters 14, 15 and 16.

The boss is a bad push: a config change that looks harmless until it isn't.
w3.l1.title: The evolution of automation
w3.l1.summary: Why automate, the five-level hierarchy, and how automation itself can hurt you.
w3.l1.body:
## The value of automation

The book lists benefits beyond "saves time": **consistency** (humans make different mistakes each time; scripts make the same one, which is fixable), **a platform** (automation can be extended, measured and reused), **faster repairs** (a system that fixes itself has lower %2%), **faster action** (machines act in milliseconds), and **time savings** (the obvious one, and the least important).

The subtle point: the value of automation compounds. A team that automates turn-up can then automate turn-down, then failover, then capacity moves. A team that does everything by hand cannot get to any of those.

## The hierarchy

%1%

%3%'s history follows this ladder: from operators running commands, to shared scripts, to generic tooling like %4% (a unit-test framework for datacenter configuration) and turn-up automation, to %5% (the cluster manager) making most of the earlier automation unnecessary. The target is the top rung: a system designed so that the failure mode does not exist, so nothing needs to be automated.

## Case study: cluster turn-up

Turning up a new cluster used to be a hundreds-of-steps checklist. %6%'s path: encode each step as a test (%7%, "does this config match reality?"), then make the tests fix what they find (idempotent turn-up), then have the cluster manager provision from a specification. Each stage removed a class of human action and a class of human error.

## Case study: the Diskerase incident

An automation that erased disks in preparation for reinstall was given an empty list of machines because of a bug in a query. The automation interpreted "no machines listed" as "all machines" and wiped a serving cluster. Lessons the book draws:

- Automation must **fail safe**: an empty target list should abort, not broaden scope.
- Rate limits and blast-radius checks belong in the tool, not in the operator's head.
- Automation propagates errors as fast as it propagates fixes.

## Reliability is the fundamental feature

When automation becomes the mechanism by which the system operates (self-healing, autoscaling), a bug in it is an outage. Treat automation as production software: tests, reviews, %8%, rollbacks. The book's warning about "automation-induced skill atrophy" is also real: if operators never do the manual procedure, they cannot do it when the automation fails. Keep the manual path documented and exercised.

> [aws]**On %9%.** The ladder maps directly: console clicks (1) → team shell scripts (2) → SSM Automation documents and %10%/%11% (3) → %12% rules invoking SSM Automation or %13% when a %14% alarm fires, %15%, %16% %17% auto-remediation (4) → managed services that eliminate the failure mode (%18% Multi-AZ failover, %19% Serverless, %20% durability) (5). Guardrails for the Diskerase lesson: require explicit resource lists, use %21% conditions to restrict what automation may touch, tag-scoped permissions, and dry-run modes. Test automation in a sandbox account with the same %22% boundaries as production.

## When not to automate

- The task is genuinely one-off and cheap.
- The system is about to be replaced.
- The automation would be more complex than the manual task and used rarely (keep a documented procedure instead).
- You cannot make it fail safe. Then, automate the check but leave the action to a human.
w3.l1.q0.q: Arrange the levels of the automation hierarchy from lowest (least automated) to highest.
w3.l1.q0.explain: The ladder climbs from manual work through shared tooling to systems where the failure mode no longer exists.
w3.l1.q0.i0: No automation: a human performs every step
w3.l1.q0.i4: Systems that do not need automation
w3.l1.q1.q: What is the primary lesson of the Diskerase incident?
w3.l1.q1.explain: An empty target list was interpreted as "everything". Scope checks and rate limits inside the tool prevent that class of error.
w3.l1.q1.c1: Automation must fail safe: ambiguous or empty inputs should abort, and blast-radius limits belong in the tool
w3.l1.q1.c2: Queries should be written in SQL
w3.l1.q1.c3: Only senior engineers should run automation
w3.l1.q2.q: Which of these is the least important benefit of automation according to the book's discussion?
w3.l1.q2.explain: Time saved is the obvious benefit, but consistency, speed of repair and the compounding platform effect matter more.
w3.l1.q3.q: An %1% team has a %2% alarm that triggers an %3% rule, which runs an SSM Automation document to replace an unhealthy instance. Which rung of the ladder is that?
w3.l1.q3.explain: The system detects and acts on its own condition without a human. Level 5 would be a managed service where unhealthy instances are not your problem at all.
w3.l2.title: Release engineering
w3.l2.summary: Hermetic builds, self-service pipelines, policy enforcement and why releases are a discipline.
w3.l2.body:
## A discipline, not a chore

%1% treats release engineering as a specialty: people who understand build systems, packaging, configuration management, deployment and the interaction of all four. The book's philosophy has four parts.

- **Self-service.** Product teams control and run their own releases. Release engineering builds the tooling and policy; it does not push buttons for other teams. Anything else becomes a bottleneck and a source of %2%.
- **High velocity.** Frequent releases mean fewer changes per release, which makes testing and troubleshooting easier and rollbacks cheaper. "Push on green" (deploy every build that passes tests) is a valid strategy for many services.
- **Hermetic builds.** A build is insensitive to the libraries and tools installed on the build machine. Same source revision, same output, on any machine, at any time. This is what makes a rollback trustworthy and a cherry-pick reproducible.
- **Enforcement of policies and procedures.** Who may release, what must be reviewed, which tests gate which stage. Enforced by the pipeline, visible in an audit trail, not by convention.

## The pipeline in the book

%3%'s %4% system: branch from a known-good revision (never build releases from head for long-lived services), build hermetically, run the test suite, package into a versioned, immutable artifact (MPM packages, signed and labelled), then deploy through %5% to full fleet. Cherry-picks go onto the release branch, and each is a new build with a new version.

Key properties to copy regardless of tooling:
- **Immutable, versioned artifacts.** You deploy the thing you tested, byte for byte.
- **A single path to production.** Emergency fixes go through the same pipeline, perhaps with fewer bake-time gates, not through an SSH session.
- **Rollback as a first-class action.** Rolling back is deploying a previous artifact, with the same automation and the same monitoring.

## Configuration management

The book distinguishes four ways to handle configuration: alongside the binary in the same package; in a separate package deployed together; as a separate versioned package; or read from an external store at runtime. Each is legitimate; what matters is that config changes are versioned, reviewed, rolled out progressively and revertible exactly like code. Lesson 3.5 covers this in depth.

## Start early

The book's advice to product teams: involve release engineering at the design stage. Budgeting for release tooling after launch produces a service that can only be deployed by its original authors.

> [aws]**On %6%.** A hermetic pipeline: %7% (or GitHub Actions) building in a pinned container image, producing an immutable artifact (a container image in ECR with an immutable tag, an AMI via %8% Image Builder, or a %9% zip in %10% with a version). %11% enforces stages and approvals; %12% performs blue/green or %13% deployments to %14%, %15% or %16% with automatic rollback on alarm. Sign images (ECR image signing with %17%) and restrict deployment %18% roles so nothing reaches production outside the pipeline. Treat %19% change sets as the review artifact for infrastructure changes. "Rollback" means "deploy the previous image tag", never "fix forward in the console".

## Smells

- Builds that pass on one machine and fail on another.
- A release that requires a specific person.
- Hotfixes applied by hand and then "backported" to source later.
- %20% edited in place in production with no version.
- Rollback untested until the day it is needed.
w3.l2.q0.explain: Hermeticity makes builds reproducible, which is the foundation for trustworthy rollbacks and cherry-picks.
w3.l2.q0.c0: A build performed in a sealed datacenter
w3.l2.q0.c1: A build whose output depends only on the source revision and pinned toolchain, not on the state of the build machine
w3.l2.q0.c3: A build produced by the release engineering team rather than developers
w3.l2.q1.q: Which practices align with the book's release philosophy? Select all that apply.
w3.l2.q1.explain: Self-service, immutable artifacts, high velocity and enforced policy. SSH hotfixes bypass the single path to production.
w3.l2.q1.c0: Product teams run their own releases with tooling built by release engineering
w3.l2.q1.c1: Deploying the exact artifact that passed testing
w3.l2.q1.c2: Emergency fixes applied via SSH and backported later
w3.l2.q1.c3: Frequent small releases rather than rare large ones
w3.l2.q1.c4: Policies enforced by the pipeline rather than by convention
w3.l2.q2.q: Why does the book advise branching a release from a known-good revision rather than building from head?
w3.l2.q2.explain: A release branch isolates the release from the ongoing churn on the main line; fixes are added deliberately as new versioned builds.
w3.l2.q2.c1: Cherry-picking fixes onto a stable branch keeps unrelated in-flight changes out of the release, making it reproducible and easier to reason about
w3.l2.q2.c2: Git does not support building from head
w3.l2.q2.c3: Head is not covered by tests
w3.l2.q3.q: On %1%, which practice most directly implements "rollback as a first-class action"?
w3.l2.q3.explain: Rollback should be the same mechanism as deploy, automated and triggered by monitoring. Snapshots and wikis are not a mechanism.
w3.l2.q3.c0: Keeping the previous container image in ECR and having %1% roll back automatically to it when a %2% alarm fires during deployment
w3.l2.q3.c1: Taking an AMI snapshot before each deploy
w3.l2.q3.c2: Documenting the manual rollback steps in a wiki
w3.l2.q3.c3: Giving %1% engineers console access to fix forward
w3.l3.title: Simplicity
w3.l3.summary: Boring is good, code is a liability, and APIs should be small.
w3.l3.body:
## Stability versus agility

The book frames the tension plainly: %1% works to keep a system stable and agile at the same time, and simplicity is what makes both possible. A simple system is easier to reason about when it breaks (stability) and easier to change (agility). Complexity is where these two goals start fighting.

## The virtue of boring

Boring is a feature. Surprises in production are bad; production software should behave predictably. The book distinguishes **essential complexity** (inherent in the problem: a web server needs to serve pages fast) from **accidental complexity** (introduced by the solution: a garbage-collection pause that could be engineered away). %2% push back on accidental complexity and expect a justification for anything added to the system they support.

## "I won't give up my code!"

Unused code, dead feature flags and speculative abstractions are liabilities: they must be read, built, tested and understood. The book's suggestion of a **negative lines of code** metric is only half a joke. Deleting code is engineering; the review for a deletion should be as celebrated as the review for a feature.

## Minimal APIs

Antoine de Saint-Exupéry via the book: perfection is reached not when there is nothing left to add, but when there is nothing left to take away. A small, well-defined API with few methods and arguments is easier to keep reliable, easier to monitor, and easier to change. Every optional parameter is a code path you must test and a behaviour you must preserve forever.

## Modularity

Loose coupling between binaries, and between binary and configuration, lets teams change parts independently. Versioned APIs let clients migrate on their own schedule. The book's point: modularity in the *system* is what allows small, frequent, safe releases at the *process* level.

## Release simplicity

Small releases are easier to measure, roll back and reason about. If a release with 100 changes causes a regression, finding it means bisecting 100 changes. If it has one, the search is over. Simplicity in the release process is the same virtue as simplicity in the code.

> [aws]**On %3%.** Accidental complexity accumulates in the account, not just the code: unused security groups, forgotten %4% versions, three ways to deploy the same service, five overlapping %5% roles. Periodic deletion is reliability work. Prefer fewer, boring services you understand deeply over many novel ones. When a design review proposes a new component, the question is not "is it cool" but "which failure mode does it add, and who gets paged for it".

## A simplicity checklist for design reviews

- Which part of this is essential, and which is accidental?
- What is the smallest API that solves the problem?
- What can be deleted to make room for this?
- Can this be released in pieces?
- Who will understand this at 3 a.m.?
w3.l3.q0.q: What distinguishes essential from accidental complexity?
w3.l3.q0.explain: %1% should expect a justification for accidental complexity and push to remove it.
w3.l3.q0.c0: Essential complexity is in the code; accidental is in the infrastructure
w3.l3.q0.c1: Essential complexity is inherent in the problem; accidental complexity is introduced by a particular solution and can be engineered away
w3.l3.q0.c2: Essential complexity is what %1% handle; accidental is for developers
w3.l3.q1.q: Why does the book treat unused code as a liability rather than a harmless asset?
w3.l3.q1.explain: Every line has a maintenance cost and a potential failure mode. Deletion is engineering work.
w3.l3.q1.c1: It must still be read, built, tested and understood, and it may contain paths that misbehave in production
w3.l3.q2.q: A release contains 80 unrelated changes and causes a latency regression. What simplicity principle would have made this cheaper to resolve?
w3.l3.q2.explain: Bisecting 80 changes is expensive; a release with one change is self-attributing.
w3.l3.q2.c1: Release simplicity: smaller, more frequent releases make regressions easy to attribute and roll back
w3.l3.q3.q: True or false: adding optional parameters to an API is a low-cost way to add flexibility, since callers who do not need them are unaffected.
w3.l3.q3.explain: False. Every optional parameter is a code path to test, monitor and preserve indefinitely. Minimal APIs are more reliable.
w3.l4.title: Canarying releases
w3.l4.summary: Progressive rollouts, %1% populations, metric selection and the analysis that decides go or no-go.
w3.l4.body:
## Why %3%

A %4% is a partial, time-limited deployment of a change, observed to decide whether the change is safe for everyone. It reduces the %5% of a bad change from "all users" to "a small, deliberately chosen fraction of users for a short time". The workbook treats %6% as a **process**, not a feature of the deployment tool: it needs a plan, metrics, a decision rule and a rollback path.

%2%

## Separate what changes at different rates

Components that change at different rates should be deployed and canaried separately: binaries, configuration, data (ML models, catalogues), and infrastructure. Bundling a config change with a binary release makes %7% analysis ambiguous: which change caused the regression?

## The %8% process

1. **Choose the %9% population.** Large enough to produce statistically meaningful metrics, small enough that a failure stays within %10%. Representative of the whole (not just one region or one customer type). Typical progression: 1 task → 1 %11% → 1 region → global.
2. **Set the duration.** Long enough to see the effects the change could plausibly have: a memory leak needs hours; a latency regression shows in minutes. Cover at least one traffic cycle for changes that interact with load.
3. **Pick the metrics.** The workbook's criteria: the metric must **indicate problems**, be **representative and attributable** to the change, and be **sensitive** (react to a small population's problems) while not being so noisy that it fires on nothing. %12% are the natural starting point; add resource metrics (memory, %13%, error logs) as leading indicators.
4. **Compare against a control.** Compare %14% tasks against baseline tasks running the old version under the same traffic and the same time window, not against last week. Without a control, a traffic surge looks like a regression.
5. **Decide.** A pre-agreed rule: if %15% error rate exceeds control by more than X, or %16% latency by more than Y, roll back automatically. Humans review borderline cases.

## Dependencies and isolation

If the %17% shares dependencies with the baseline (a database, a cache), a bad %18% can hurt the baseline population through those dependencies. Rate-limit what a %19% may do to shared resources; watch dependency metrics during the %20% too.

## Non-interactive systems

Batch jobs and pipelines cannot be canaried by traffic percentage. Options: run the new version on a fraction of the input and compare outputs; run both and diff; %21% in a staging environment with production data. The decision rule is the same.

## Requirements on monitoring

Canary analysis needs metrics that are labelled by version so %22% and control can be separated, at a resolution fine enough to see the %23% period, with low enough latency to make the rollback decision quickly. Without version labels, %24% is guesswork.

> [aws]**On %25%.** %26% provides %27% and linear deployment configurations for %28% and %29% (for example %1%, or custom percentages), with automatic rollback when specified %30% alarms enter ALARM during the deployment. For %31% with an %32%, blue/green uses two target groups with weighted routing, which gives you a clean control population. %33% aliases route a weight of traffic to a new version. For metric attribution, tag %34% tasks or %35% versions and include the version as a metric dimension. Use a **%36% composite alarm** over the %37%'s %38% as the rollback trigger. For infrastructure changes, deploy stacks to one region or one %39% first (a cellular layout makes this natural; see World 7).

## Anti-patterns

- Canarying to 50% first: half your users are not a %40%.
- No control group, so time-of-day effects masquerade as regressions.
- Judging by "no alerts fired" instead of comparing metrics.
- Bake time of 30 seconds for a change that leaks memory over hours.
- Canary in a region with no real users.
w3.l4.q0.q: Why compare %1% metrics against a concurrently running control population rather than against last week's numbers?
w3.l4.q0.explain: A concurrent control under the same traffic removes confounders. Comparing to history confuses "the change is bad" with "today is different".
w3.l4.q0.c1: Traffic, time of day and dependency behaviour differ over time; a concurrent control isolates the effect of the change
w3.l4.q1.q: Which metric properties does the workbook require for %1% analysis? Select all that apply.
w3.l4.q1.explain: Metrics must be problem-indicating, attributable and sensitive. They must also be labelled by version and available during the %1%, not after.
w3.l4.q1.c1: Representative and attributable to the change
w3.l4.q1.c2: Sensitive enough to react to a small %1% population
w3.l4.q1.c3: Available only after the deployment completes
w3.l4.q2.q: A team bundles a configuration change with a binary release and %1% both together. The %2% shows a latency regression. What is the process problem?
w3.l4.q2.explain: Separate binaries, configuration and data into separate %1% so each result is attributable.
w3.l4.q2.c1: Components that change at different rates were bundled, so the regression cannot be attributed to one change without another cycle
w3.l4.q3.q: How long should a %1% last for a change suspected of introducing a slow memory leak?
w3.l4.q3.explain: Duration must cover the effects the change could plausibly have. A leak needs hours; a routing change needs minutes.
w3.l4.q3.c0: Thirty seconds, to keep velocity high
w3.l4.q3.c1: Long enough for the leak to become visible in memory metrics, potentially hours, and ideally across a traffic cycle
w3.l4.q4.q: On %1%, which mechanism gives a clean control population for an %2% service behind an %3% during a %4%?
w3.l4.q4.explain: Two target groups serving the same traffic mix let you compare old and new under identical conditions, with rollback as a weight change.
w3.l4.q4.c0: Blue/green deployment with two target groups and weighted routing
w3.l5.title: Configuration: design and safe rollout
w3.l5.summary: %1% is code that lies about being data. Design it, validate it, roll it out like a binary.
w3.l5.body:
## Why configuration is dangerous

Configuration changes bypass most of the safeguards built for code: they often skip tests, they can be applied instantly fleet-wide, and they are frequently edited under time pressure during incidents. A large share of the outages in the workbook's case studies are config pushes. Two chapters address it: how to design configuration, and how to deploy it.

## Configuration philosophy (workbook ch.14)

- **Configuration asks questions of the user.** Every knob is a question the operator must answer. Minimise the questions; make the defaults right for most users; distinguish **mandatory** questions (what must be set) from **optional** tuning.
- **Optimise for the reader**, not the writer. %1% will be read during outages far more often than written.
- **Separate config from code**, but keep it versioned, reviewed and testable like code. A change to a config file should have a diff, a reviewer, and a rollout.
- **Ownership.** Each config value has an owner who understands its effect. Orphaned settings are a hazard.
- **Guard against the "everything is a knob" design.** Exposing internals as tunables invites operators to work around bugs instead of fixing them, and creates combinations nobody tested.

## Configuration specifics (workbook ch.15)

- **Validate before applying.** Syntax, schema, and semantic checks (does this reference an existing resource; is this timeout shorter than the caller's deadline).
- **Test configuration.** Unit tests for config (the %2% idea from lesson 3.1), and integration tests that load the config into the real binary.
- **Roll out progressively**, exactly like a binary: %3%, observe, expand, with rollback. "It's just a config change" is the most expensive sentence in operations.
- **Make it revertible**: keep the previous version, and make rollback a one-step action.
- **Version-pin what the config references** (image tags, schema versions) so a config rollback is coherent.
- **Beware of config that changes behaviour in a loop**: a config-driven autoscaler pushed fleet-wide can amplify a mistake instantly.

## Feature flags

Flags are config with a shorter lifetime. The same rules apply, plus: flags must have an owner and a removal date; long-lived flags become undocumented configuration; flag evaluation must be cheap and fail safe (a missing flag service should not take the site down: default to the last known value).

> [aws]**On %4%.** %5% %6% exists for this problem: it stores configuration and feature flags with **validators** (JSON Schema or %7%), and deploys them using **deployment strategies** (percentage of targets over a bake time) with automatic rollback when a %8% alarm fires during the deployment. %9% and %10% handle simpler values and secrets, with versioning. For infrastructure config, %11% change sets give a diff before apply, and stack policies limit what a change may touch. Never edit a running task definition, %12% environment variable or security group by hand in production; that is an unversioned config push.

## A config change checklist

1. Is there a diff, and has someone else read it?
2. Was it validated against a schema and loaded by the binary in a test?
3. Does the rollout go to a %13% first, with a bake time and a decision rule?
4. Is the previous version one action away?
5. Who owns this value, and is the effect documented where the %14% engineer will find it?
w3.l5.q0.q: Why does the workbook argue that configuration changes deserve the same rollout discipline as binary changes?
w3.l5.q0.explain: %1% skips most safeguards by default. Canarying, validation and one-step rollback restore them.
w3.l5.q0.c0: Because config files are larger than binaries
w3.l5.q0.c1: Because config changes can alter behaviour fleet-wide instantly while bypassing tests and review, which makes them a leading cause of outages
w3.l5.q0.c3: Because config cannot be rolled back
w3.l5.q1.q: Which of these are recommended practices for configuration? Select all that apply.
w3.l5.q1.explain: Everything-is-a-knob creates untested combinations and invites working around bugs. The rest are the workbook's core recommendations.
w3.l5.q1.c0: Validate against a schema and semantic checks before applying
w3.l5.q1.c1: Expose every internal tunable so operators can adapt quickly
w3.l5.q1.c2: Optimise the format for readers rather than writers
w3.l5.q2.q: A feature-flag service becomes unreachable. What is the fail-safe behaviour for the application?
w3.l5.q2.explain: Flag evaluation must be cheap and fail safe. A configuration dependency should never be able to take the site down.
w3.l5.q2.c0: Crash, so the outage is visible
w3.l5.q2.c2: Use the last known flag values (or the compiled-in defaults) and continue serving
w3.l5.q2.c3: Stop serving until the flag service returns
w3.l5.q3.q: Which %1% service provides validators plus percentage-based deployment strategies with alarm-triggered rollback specifically for configuration and feature flags?
w3.l5.q3.explain: %1% is built for progressive, validated configuration rollout. %2% %3% (a different service) audits resource compliance; %4% stores values but does not roll them out progressively.
w3.boss.title: The Bad Push
w3.boss.tagline: A one-line config change. What could go wrong.
w3.boss.intro:
You are %1% for **Search**, a query API on %2% behind an %3%, with an Elasticsearch-compatible cluster behind it. %4%: 99.9% of queries succeed within 800 ms, 30-day window. Budget remaining: 62%.

A developer wants to ship a change to the query timeout config: from 2000 ms down to 400 ms, "to stop slow queries from hogging threads". Configuration is stored in %5% and deployed by a pipeline. Play the change through.
w3.boss.win:
The timeout change shipped, cut thread-pool saturation in half, and cost no %1%. The difference between this and an outage was treating a one-line config change as a change: data before deciding the value, a %2% with a decision rule, attribution before proceeding, and a safe default path for the next one.

**Takeaway:** the question is never "is this change small"; it is "how fast can it hurt everyone, and how fast can I undo it".
w3.boss.lose:
The "harmless" config push breached the %1% or left the pipeline unsafe for the next one. Typical failure paths: approving on "config only", setting a timeout from opinion instead of the latency histogram, deploying fleet-wide, skipping stages, or reverting the pipeline to instant 100% rollouts.

Revisit lessons 3.4 and 3.5 and retry.
w3.boss.s0.text: The pull request changes a single value in the config JSON: %1%. The description says "low risk, config only". The pipeline's config stage currently deploys to 100% of tasks immediately, no bake time.
w3.boss.s0.c0.text: Before approving, ask what fraction of successful queries currently take longer than 400 ms (from the latency histogram), and require the change to go through a %1% deployment strategy with a bake time.
w3.boss.s0.c0.fb: Correct: a timeout is a policy that turns slow successes into failures. Check the histogram first; a 400 ms timeout with a %1% of 600 ms would fail 5% of queries. Then treat it as a real rollout.
w3.boss.s0.c1.text: Approve. It is a one-line config change with an obvious intent.
w3.boss.s0.c1.fb: "%1% only" is the most expensive sentence in operations. Fleet-wide, instantly, untested.
w3.boss.s0.c2.text: Reject: timeouts should never be changed.
w3.boss.s0.c2.fb: The intent (protect threads from slow queries) is legitimate. The job is to make the change safe, not to block it.
w3.boss.s1.text: The histogram shows about 1.8% of successful queries take over 400 ms, mostly complex facet queries from one enterprise customer. The developer proposes 400 ms anyway: "those queries are abusive".
w3.boss.s1.c0.text: Point out that 1.8% failures would be 18× the %1% rate; propose a timeout around %2% (roughly 900 ms) plus a separate per-customer concurrency limit for the heavy tenant, and validate the value against the caller's own deadline.
w3.boss.s1.c0.fb: Timeouts must be set from data, and the per-tenant problem is a per-tenant control (quotas or a separate pool), not a global timeout that breaks everyone with legitimate slow queries.
w3.boss.s1.c1.text: Agree to 400 ms because the customer is being abusive.
w3.boss.s1.c1.fb: You just planned an %1% breach. 1.8% errors against a 0.1% budget exhausts 30 days of budget in under two days.
w3.boss.s1.c2.text: Set it to 400 ms but only for that customer.
w3.boss.s1.c2.fb: Closer to a per-tenant control, but a per-customer timeout still converts their legitimate slow queries into errors that count against your %1%. Concurrency limits or a separate pool are cleaner.
w3.boss.s2.text: Agreed: timeout 900 ms, and a tenant concurrency limit later. You configure the %1% deployment strategy. Options on the table.
w3.boss.s2.c0.text: Deploy to 10% of tasks with a 20-minute bake, monitored by a composite alarm on the %1% (error rate and %2% latency, %3% vs baseline), with automatic rollback if the alarm fires. Then 50%, then 100%.
w3.boss.s2.c0.fb: A real %1%: small population, meaningful bake time, SLI-based decision rule, automated rollback. Version-labelled metrics make the comparison possible.
w3.boss.s2.c1.text: Deploy to 100% with a 5-minute bake and watch the dashboard.
w3.boss.s2.c1.fb: A 100% deployment is not a %1%, and "watch the dashboard" is not a decision rule.
w3.boss.s2.c2.text: Deploy to 1 task and watch for 1 minute, then go to 100%.
w3.boss.s2.c2.fb: One task for one minute produces almost no signal on a 0.1% budget, and the jump to 100% skips the stages that would catch a partial problem.
w3.boss.s3.text: Canary at 10%. The composite alarm shows: error rate %1% 0.04% vs baseline 0.03%; %2% latency %3% 720 ms vs baseline 1450 ms. Thread-pool saturation on %4% tasks dropped from 85% to 40%.
w3.boss.s3.c0.text: Proceed to 50%: error rate is within noise of baseline, latency improved as intended, and the saturation signal confirms the mechanism. Keep the bake time for the next stage.
w3.boss.s3.c0.fb: The data supports the change on all chosen metrics and the effect is explained. Continue the staged rollout without skipping bake times.
w3.boss.s3.c1.text: Roll back: the error rate went up.
w3.boss.s3.c1.fb: 0.04% vs 0.03% on a 10% %1% over 20 minutes is noise; the decision rule should have a threshold well above that. Rolling back on noise trains people to ignore the rule.
w3.boss.s3.c2.text: Jump straight to 100%; the %1% looks great.
w3.boss.s3.c2.fb: The 50% stage exists to catch effects that only appear at scale (shared dependency load, cache behaviour). Skipping it discards the cheapest information you have.
w3.boss.s4.text: At 50%, the %1% shows a small spike in %2% from a single %3% for two minutes, then it recovers. The composite alarm did not fire. A developer says: "Unrelated; that %4% had a node replacement. Push to 100%."
w3.boss.s4.c0.text: Pause the rollout, verify the spike correlates with the node replacement event (and not the config version dimension) before proceeding, and note it in the change log.
w3.boss.s4.c0.fb: Attribution is the whole point of %1% analysis. Five minutes to check the version dimension against the %2% event keeps the rollout decision evidence-based.
w3.boss.s4.c1.text: Push to 100% on the developer's word.
w3.boss.s4.c1.fb: Maybe it was the node replacement. Or maybe the timeout interacts with that %1%'s slower storage. You will not know until 100% of users find out.
w3.boss.s4.c2.fb: Defensible but expensive: the alarm did not fire and there is a plausible explanation to verify first. Pause, check, then decide.
w3.boss.s5.text: Verified: the spike was the node replacement (same spike on baseline tasks in that %1%). Rollout completes to 100%. The developer now wants to change the %2% deployment strategy back to "100%, no bake" for future config changes "because most changes are trivial".
w3.boss.s5.c0.text: Keep the staged strategy as the default for all config, with a documented expedited path (smaller bake, still canaried) for emergencies. Add a validator so out-of-range timeouts are rejected before deployment.
w3.boss.s5.c0.fb: The safe path must be the default path. Validators catch the next fat-finger; the expedited path keeps emergencies from bypassing the process entirely.
w3.boss.s5.c1.text: Agree: staged rollouts for config are overhead.
w3.boss.s5.c1.fb: You have just re-armed the exact failure mode this scenario was about, for every future config change.
w3.boss.s5.c2.text: Require manual %1% approval for every config change instead.
w3.boss.s5.c2.fb: That is a human gate that becomes %1% and a bottleneck. Automated validation and staged rollout scale; approvals do not.
